en.title: Lanterns Episode 2: Hal Jordan's Powerless Plight Fuels a Cosmic Mystery
en.summary: Stripped of his iconic ring and forced into detective work, Hal Jordan navigates a compelling sci-fi mystery in 'Lanterns' second episode. The show proves its strength lies not just in cosmic battles, but in its character-driven narrative.
en.body:
The second episode of **Lanterns**, titled "Trust Fall," wastes no time in challenging its titular hero. Just minutes into the episode, **Hal Jordan**'s power ring fizzles out, leaving him without his signature cosmic abilities. This unexpected turn sends **John Stewart** on a mission to retrieve Hal's charger from Coast City, while Hal is left to investigate a series of murders in Rushville using decidedly more earthly methods. It’s a bold narrative choice that echoes classic Green Lantern lore, where power isn't always the answer, forcing Hal to rely on his wits and detective skills.

Directed by **James Hawes** and penned by **Vanessa Baden Kelly** and showrunner **Chris Mundy**, "Trust Fall" effectively pivots from the initial introductions of the series. While the first episode laid the groundwork, this installment delves into a compelling alien mystery. Hal's investigation in Rushville, which involves a rather grim examination of the victims at the morgue, highlights the gritty, noir-esque potential of the series. It’s a stark contrast to the usual space opera adventures, proving that **Lanterns** can be just as engaging when its heroes are grounded, even if that grounding is temporarily literal.

## A New Kind of Investigation

The episode's strength lies in its ability to craft a captivating narrative even when its protagonist is stripped of his powers. The source material, specifically **Green Lantern #192** from 1985, featured a powerless Hal facing down Star Sapphire, demonstrating his resilience beyond the ring. While "Trust Fall" doesn't directly adapt that comic moment, it captures a similar spirit. Hal's fearlessness in the face of vulnerability is a core aspect of his character, and this episode allows that trait to shine without the crutch of his immense power. The mystery surrounding the victims and their connection to larger alien forces sets a compelling stage for the unfolding season.

## The Weight of Expectation

For fans of the **Green Lantern** franchise, seeing Hal Jordan operate without his ring is a significant departure. It signifies a willingness from the showrunners to explore the characters on a deeper level, examining their resolve and ingenuity when their primary tools are unavailable. This approach resonates with the core of what makes these characters compelling: their humanity and their unwavering commitment to justice, regardless of the odds or their power levels. The journey to Oa and the eventual confrontation with **Sinestro** promise a return to more familiar epic stakes, but the detour through Hal's powerless investigation adds a crucial layer of depth that binge-watchers will surely appreciate.

## What's Next

With Hal's ring recharged and the investigation pointing towards off-world implications, the next episode is poised to escalate the conflict. The looming presence of **Sinestro** suggests a direct confrontation with a major antagonist, and the alien mystery introduced in "Trust Fall" is likely to expand, bringing the **Green Lantern Corps** fully into the fray.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for Lanterns season 1 episode 2. A t the start of Green Lantern #192 (1985), by Steve Englehart and Joe Staton, the supervillain Star Sapphire carries Hal Jordan into the air and drops him. Despite the fact that Hal no longer wears a power ring, having rescinded his membership in the Green Lantern Corps months earlier, he remains unafraid. He looks around as he plummets, searching for a way to continue his mission, despite the fact that he no longer has superpowers. Nothing from that issue appears in the second episode of Lanterns , “Trust Fall,” but it’s hard not to recall that scene of a powerless Hal. The episode strips Hal of his power almost immediately, having his ring run out of charge in the first 10 minutes and sending John on a mission back to Coast City, California, to retrieve his battery to recharge. And yet, it still finds ways to be a compelling sci-fi mystery, even if Green Lantern can’t be Green Lantern. Now that introductions are out of the way—including, it should be said, the death of Hal Jordan in 2026, something that episode two doesn’t even mention—”Trust Fall” can spend more time doing what Lanterns really wants to do, probing an alien mystery. Directed by James Hawes and written by Vanessa Baden Kelly and showrunner Chris Mundy, the episode spends most of its time sending Hal and John on separate missions before building to a trip off-planet to visit Sinestro, the big bad of the Green Lantern franchise. Before flying to the Green Lantern Corps headquarters on the planet Oa, Hal plays the gumshoe in Rushville. That means breaking into the morgue and dragging the (very naked) victims of last week’s shootings through the metal-detectors around town, which reveal themselves to be alien detectors. These sequences also give Hal more time alone with Sheriff Kerry, a pairing that’s good for plot purposes, but even better for letting viewers enjoy the chemistry between the two. Even thirty years after Trainspotting , it’s easy to underestimate Kelly Macdonald, who seemed like a shy bumpkin out of her depth in the pilot, only to reveal herself as more than capable in “Trust Fall.” When she dresses down Hal for treating the fruit of his labor as a big revelation about aliens in the town, telling him, “Congratulations, you’re now caught up to me,” the viewer feels as if she’s talking to us too. For his part, John gets sent across the country to retrieve Hal’s power battery. Although Hal calls it another training mission, John correctly realizes that Hal wants him out of the way. Annoying as that may be for Hal, it’s good news for us, because this segment indulges in a lot of deep Green Lantern lore, including name dropping a classic Alan Moore story, showing Hal’s battery hidden in a pocket dimension, and a look at Earl, Hal’s alien plant and a nod to Itty, the pet sidekick Hal had in
